repos.title: Solv3R: 3D Looped Transformer as a Multi-view Solver
repos.paper_summary:
Solv3R reformulates multi-view 3D reconstruction as a stationary looped transformer solver: one shared update operator is applied at every call, independent of how many calls a view has already received. It is fine-tuned from the pretrained DéjàView model, with learned constant gates replacing iteration-conditioned gates and the state rescaled to a fixed RMS norm after each update. Training uses random gradient-free solver calls, differentiable calls supervised after 24 to 48 calls, Gaussian noise or partial resets, and distillation of DéjàView outputs after 16 calls.

On the offline benchmarks in Table 1 (DTU, ETH3D, 7-Scenes, ScanNet++, nuScenes), Solv3R with 16 fixed calls reaches camera AUC@30 of 99.0 on DTU and 94.8 on ETH3D, close to DéjàView's 98.8 and 95.4. Adaptive stopping, which halts when the relative state update falls below γ = 0.02, uses 91.3 TFLOPs for 24 views, versus 75.9 for DéjàView at 16 calls. Under perturbation, Solv3R recovers accurate poses where DéjàView does not.

Limitations: the stability and correction results come from selected windows, and the stopping rule's reliability on other datasets appears only in the supplement. Solv3R's behavior beyond 64 calls is not reported in the main text.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Feed-forward geometric models struggle to refine or extend reconstructions, so the paper proposes Solv3R, a reusable learned solver.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans feed-forward geometry, looped refinement and streaming reconstruction, which Solv3R applies as one solver.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A stationary learned update, trained for stability, correction and continuation, is shared across all solver calls.

digest_headlines.heading: Solver analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Solv3R's camera error stays low as updates shrink and recovers after perturbation, unlike DéjàView.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Solv3R's accuracy at 16 calls is comparable to DéjàView, and it is competitive across offline, incremental, relocalization and streaming tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion argues that a single learned solver can unify offline, incremental, relocalization and streaming reconstruction.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists implementation details, evaluation protocols, extra analyses, a failure case and additional aerial and qualitative results.

repos.title: RobotAgentBench: Towards Open-world Robot Autonomy
repos.paper_summary: RobotAgentBench (RAB) is a simulation benchmark for evaluating robot agents on open-world household tasks. An agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline builds 50 layouts in Isaac Sim, with 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks, and 4 open-ended scenarios. Tasks test five capabilities: task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and disturbance handling. Scenarios test end-to-end progress. Eleven standalone VLA/WAM policies and five agent architectures run on the same 22-dimensional command interface, with 30 instances per task or scenario. The best standalone policy, InternVLA-A1.5, averages 18.0 on task-level scores. The best agent, a code planner and verifier that calls both code and learned policies (C/H/C), averages 48.5 and scores 15.4 on open-ended scenarios, versus 2.0 for the best standalone model there. Recursive self-improvement raises the code-only Codex harness from 31.0 to 42.3 on the task-level average. Limitations: all results are simulated, real-world results are described only qualitatively, and open-ended scores remain low.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Current benchmarks test isolated manipulation skills, so this work proposes a benchmark for full robot autonomy in household settings.

digest_headlines.heading: RobotAgentBench
digest_headlines.headline: Real rooms are rebuilt in simulation to create 50 layouts, and five agent architectures are compared under one framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Standalone policies average at most 18.0, while the best agent, a hybrid code and learned-policy design, reaches 48.5.

repos.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
repos.paper_summary: SpecPilot is an autonomous agentic loop that searches for lossless speculative decoding optimizations tailored to each deployment. A cost model ranks the largest gaps between the current system and an estimated speedup ceiling, parallel agents explore directions on separate GPUs, and a controller promotes only changes with a significant gain on unseen requests. Token forcing checks every output token against the stock engine, catching lossy changes that task accuracy misses. Validated mechanisms are stored in structured memory and reused across rounds and deployments. Discovered mechanisms include W12, a lossless 12-bit weight format averaging 12.01–12.02 bits per weight; best-first tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets; two-level verification using an 8-bit view of W12 as a low-precision pre-check; and three batching mechanisms. Across four target models, three drafters, two GPUs and five benchmarks, speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding rises from stock's 4.46× to 10.87× with one request, and from 1.94× to 3.93× with batching. On H100 with one request, the paper reports 1.84× faster than DDTree. The gains are reported without training or quality loss. Limitations: the loop depends on agent-driven search, and results are measured only on the listed models, drafters, GPUs and benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Stock parallel-drafter systems leave speedup unrealized, which motivates SpecPilot's per-deployment search.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Lossless speculative decoding accepts only tokens matching the exact target's argmax, so output tests cannot easily verify it.

digest_headlines.heading: SpecPilot
digest_headlines.headline: A cost model finds the largest gap to a ceiling, and a controller accepts changes only on confirmed gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Discovered Lossless Algorithms
digest_headlines.headline: SpecPilot discovered a lossless 12-bit weight format, best-first tree verification, two-level verification and batching mechanisms.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Sealed finals on unseen requests give single-request gains of 2.13× to 2.44× and batching gains of 1.85× to 3.11×.

repos.title: PhysAg3D: Bridging 3D Generative and Agentic Models for High-Fidelity and Physically-Interactive Assets
repos.paper_summary: PhysAg3D generates interactive 3D assets from a single image by coupling a pretrained 3D generator with a vision-language agent that builds executable physical models. The agent infers semantic and physical priors from the image, while TRELLIS.2 produces a textured whole-object mesh. A hierarchical representation links requirements, physical mechanisms (rigid joints or compliant domains), and the visible surfaces that implement them. The agent constructs parts, joints, and surface bindings, then revises them using rendered views and MuJoCo execution checks, with at most two builder repairs. On 50 in-the-wild objects with 110 actions, PhysAg3D reaches 91.3% Action Completion Rate and 88.0% Function-and-Visible-Stability Pass, versus 66.8% and 42.0% for the strongest baseline, aDSL. On PhysXVerse and PhysX-Mobility it improves PSNR over the strongest baseline by 2.74 and 2.76 dB. The paper states that recovering hidden structure and material properties remains a limitation. Stability is judged from rendered video, not simulator logs, and ear-pad compliance uses an approximate model.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: PhysAg3D pairs a 3D generator with a vision-language agent that builds revisable interaction mechanisms on the generated mesh.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans image-to-3D generation, articulation prediction, agentic asset modeling, and simulation substrates.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method links an image-derived interaction hierarchy to construction and bounded refinement, with rigid and compliant bindings to visible surfaces.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: PhysAg3D leads most reported metrics across four evaluations, and ablations support bounded refinement and surface preservation.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion restates the hierarchical representation and names recovering hidden structure and material properties as a remaining limitation.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists representation details, binding checks, runtime budgets, motion-range and deformation criteria, output selection, and evaluation definitions.

repos.title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
repos.paper_summary:
HALO is a humanoid autonomy system trained on synthetic vision-language-motion data generated across 1,000 procedurally generated homes, with no human teleoperation. Its three onboard layers are a VLM orchestrator that splits free-form requests into subtasks, a motion generator that maps an egocentric RGB image and the active subtask to a 5-second whole-body kinematic plan, and a depth-conditioned tracker trained by distilling privileged PPO experts and then fine-tuning with multi-critic PPO.

On six single skills (go-to, sit, door, crouch, crawl, push), mean success is 91% in 6,000 simulated trials and 91% in 360 real-world trials across six environments not seen in training. Three chained multi-step tasks reach a mean of 69% in simulation and 70% in one real environment. In ablations on sit, training-time continuity conditioning gives 84%, versus 66% with inference-time real-time chunking and 24% without chunking. Removing depth lowers sit to 74%.

Limitations: chained success falls below the product of single-task rates (71% against 89% for Door→Go-To) because the next subtask often begins with its target out of view. The paper suggests adding search and turn-in-place recovery behaviors as a fix.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Humanoid robots need paired vision-language-motion data, which HALO generates in simulation instead of by teleoperation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work relies on scanned rooms, authored templates, or blind trackers; HALO pairs procedural homes with a perceptive tracker.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: A frozen vision-language encoder and a flow-matching decoder generate 5-second motion plans that a depth-conditioned tracker executes.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Single-task success averages 91% in simulation and reality, while chained multi-task success falls to 69% and 70%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Simulation can supply humanoid training data, but task authoring, contact sensing, the generator-tracker interface and orchestration remain limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix details the six-skill corpus, scene generation, baking error, motion filtering, rendering and generator and tracker design.

repos.title: HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvement for Harness Token Efficiency
repos.paper_summary: HarnessMM reduces repeated reasoning calls in agent harnesses by storing already-resolved actions as executable decision graphs and replaying them when tool feedback satisfies public guards, with recursive self-improvement refining companion harness configurations. A controller sits at the model–tool boundary and keeps model weights fixed. The method reuses stored actions, with literal arguments, causal dependencies and guards, and calls the original actor again when a new semantic decision, unsupported evidence or abstention occurs. On 98 HumanEval tasks, Codex keeps 90.82% success while Tokens/task (k) fall from 66.72 to 47.02 (29.54% saving). DeepSeek Harness rises from 71.43% to 85.71% success while Tokens/task (k) fall from 96.28 to 11.62 (87.93% saving). On MBPP, the Qwen-backed DeepSeek Harness rises from 90.27% to 91.83% with Tokens/task (k) falling from 53.98 to 10.61. The paper's stated limitations are that savings depend on provider cache and context accounting, that new semantic decisions still require slow reasoning, and that public-state adapters are task specific. Small development sets leave policy-level quality differences uncertain.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Harnesses re-invoke reasoning after each tool result, even when earlier reasoning already fixed the next action.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior methods reduce, route or reuse calls, while HarnessMM targets whether a future reasoning call must recur.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Substitution saves cost only when removed reasoning tokens exceed the tokens introduced by authorship, routing and fallback.

digest_headlines.heading: HarnessMM: Reusing Decisions
digest_headlines.headline: Guarded reuse executes stored actions only when public guards hold, and otherwise returns control to the original actor.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On 98 HumanEval test tasks, HarnessMM keeps Codex success at 90.82% and raises DeepSeek Harness success to 85.71%.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Savings depend on provider accounting and resolved-action availability, and adapters are task specific.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Stored, guard-checked decisions can replace repeated reasoning calls, and companion studies keep their own scope.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives per-iteration MiniWoB++ RSI measurements, development protocols, implementation details and paired-effect definitions.

repos.title: CoworkOS:Scaling Agent Coworkers for Real-world Automation
repos.paper_summary: CoworkOS is an agent harness for long-horizon human-agent work. Its three layers are a Main Agent that chooses actions, delegations, and acceptance; a Coordinator Runtime that routes messages and tracks state; and optional Subagents that run in isolated contexts, synchronously or asynchronously. Humans and agents edit the same versioned resources (documents, presentations, CAD models, Blender scenes). A commit rule checks each edit's base revision and returns a conflict for stale edits. Persistent workspaces, semantic memory, and background Jobs with logs let work resume after interruption. The paper reports competitiveness with OpenHands, Codex, and DeepSeek Harness across 12 benchmarks and six application categories, but the text gives no per-benchmark scores for these comparisons. In a post-training case study, CoworkOS ran five rounds on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and the average over eight benchmarks rose from 33.19 to 42.95 (+9.76). Limitations: the study covers one model, the authors state that gains vary across tasks, and the benchmark count is 12 in the abstract but 10 in one figure caption.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: CoworkOS splits task strategy from execution so one agent can handle complex delivery and long-horizon monitoring.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries: Task Formulation and Agency
digest_headlines.headline: Agent tasks are defined by objective, environment, actions, acceptance, and budget, judged along complexity and temporal extent.

digest_headlines.heading: The CoworkOS Agent Harness
digest_headlines.headline: A three-layer harness with synchronous or asynchronous delegation, shared application objects, and durable workspaces and memory.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: CoworkOS ranks among the top two harnesses in every domain average, leading Productivity and ML Coding.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Post-training gains vary across tasks, and the paper concludes that one harness supports productivity, monitoring, and model improvement.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists benchmark settings, scoring rules, case inspection protocols, and post-training run records with complete round scores.

repos.title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation
repos.paper_summary: Wave Forcing (WF) is a chunk-wise autoregressive method for streaming video generation that starts the next video chunk's denoising before the previous chunk finishes. Each denoising stage and a cache-refresh stage run on separate full-model replicas, so one completed chunk emerges per forward round after pipeline fill. Chunk-wise causal attention lets newer chunks read earlier, cleaner chunks. A three-stage training recipe (mixed-noise distribution-matching distillation, teacher-guided motion supervision with LPIPS, and on-policy adaptation with self-generated history) adapts Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B to this context. The Wave Runtime implements early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, 5-step WF reaches a VBench Total of 81.64 versus 81.15 for Rolling Forcing, and Dynamic Degree rises from 51.39 to 94.44 on short videos. 4-step WF reaches 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, a 7.07× speedup over a 19.06-FPS single-GPU baseline. Across six model scales (1.3B–14B), Wave Parallelism reaches 1.025–2.530× the throughput of the faster context-parallel baseline under Sage+W8A8. Limitations: VBench does not capture long-stream subject loss or camera drift, so the paper adds Subject Preservation and Camera Drift on a 100-prompt subset. Aggregate timings do not isolate VAE bottlenecks, and the gap to context parallelism narrows at 14B.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Wave Forcing targets one chunk per forward round and reports 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Sequential chunk generation needs S denoising forwards plus one store forward, so even one-step denoising takes two passes.

digest_headlines.heading: Wave Forcing
digest_headlines.headline: Chunk-wise causal attention lets newer chunks read earlier, cleaner chunks before those finish denoising.

digest_headlines.heading: Wave Runtime
digest_headlines.headline: Wave Runtime publishes key-value data early from stage-owned replicas, overlapping transfers with computation to cut waits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Five-step Wave Forcing scores 81.64 VBench Total against 81.15 for Rolling Forcing, with higher motion and subject retention.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans streaming video training, blockwise diffusion in language and robotics, and parallel execution baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Subject and drift diagnostics rely on a 100-prompt subset, and output-path decoding capacity remains unresolved.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Future work targets end-to-end profiling, mid-generation prompt changes, and interactive world models, none yet evaluated.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Jointly designing context, training, and execution yields one chunk per forward round after fill with comparable overall quality.

digest_headlines.heading: AI Use Statement
digest_headlines.headline: AI assistants supported framing, organization, editing, and figure work, and the authors remain responsible for the claims.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training schedules and loss details, runtime buffer and cache semantics, the same-graph proof, parameter configurations, and extended future work.

repos.title: Möbius: A Unified Motion-Language Model Bridging Understanding and Generation
repos.paper_summary: Möbius is a unified motion-language model that runs the full motion diffusion process inside the same multimodal attention space as text and motion understanding, rather than conditioning an external diffusion module on language-model features. It operates on continuous frame-level raw motion (D=201) with no discrete tokenizer or pretrained motion VAE. Training is two-stage: motion captioning first, then generation with the understanding parameters frozen. On HumanML3D text-to-motion, Möbius-0.6B reports R@1 0.821 and FID 6.13, versus 0.671 and 21.0 for MotionGPT3, the strongest unified baseline in Table 1. The 1.7B variant, trained on 1,700 hours of motion data, reports FID 10.7. Motion captioning (Table 2) reports BLEU-4 0.203 for the 0.6B model against 0.161 for MotionGPT3. On MotionFix editing, the 0.6B variant with additional MotionFix data reports FID 0.0955 against 0.134 for MotionLab. Limitations stated by the authors: experiments cover only controlled single-person motion, with multi-person interaction, detailed hand motion, and retargeting left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius runs the entire motion diffusion process inside the shared multimodal space used for understanding, not an external module.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior unified motion models either tokenize motion or hand language features to an external diffusion module.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius uses raw frame-level motion with role-specific parameters and shared attention, trained understanding-first.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius-0.6B scores 0.8209 on top-1 retrieval and 6.1291 on Fréchet distance, ahead of unified baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude the shared space works at 1.7B scale, with evidence limited to controlled single-person motion.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists datasets, architecture and training settings, task construction, inference settings, timing, evaluation protocols, and extra completion results.

repos.title: FastAFD: When Does Attention-FFN Disaggregation Pay on Rack-Scale NVLink?
repos.paper_summary: FastAFD is an attention–FFN disaggregation (AFD) decode engine for a GB200 NVL72 rack. It places attention on attention GPUs and MoE experts on dedicated FFN nodes, and overlaps one microbatch's MoE with the other's attention. It is compared against colocated vLLM wide expert parallelism, with the EP width tuned per workload, on three MoE models: MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3-235B, and Qwen3.5-397B. Under standard decoding, the all-GPU speedup over the best wide EP, counting FFN GPUs, is 0.99–1.17×. Qwen3 reaches 1.17× at 16K, Qwen3.5 reaches 1.16× at 4K and falls to 0.99× at 16K, and MiniMax-M2.5 is at parity (1.00–1.02×). Speculative decoding (draft depth 3, acceptance fixed near 1.8 tokens per step, simulated) raises MiniMax-M2.5 to 1.08×. An analytical model calibrated from colocated vLLM profiles predicts AFD throughput within 3% on average. The speedup factors into batch gain, overlap gain, and disaggregation cost. Limitations: results cover one rack, FP8 models, and decode only with prefill excluded, and draft acceptance is simulated. The 2.48× figure for heterogeneous SRAM-based expert placement is an ideal projection, not a measurement.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Whether AFD beats wide EP on GB200 NVL72 is unsettled, so the paper builds FastAFD and benchmarks it against tuned wide EP.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Colocated wide EP already frees much of the memory AFD targets, so the comparison must charge AFD for its FFN nodes.

digest_headlines.heading: End-to-End Performance on NVL72
digest_headlines.headline: Against tuned wide EP, FastAFD reaches 0.99–1.17× all-GPU speedup under standard decoding and 1.02–1.13× under speculative decoding.

digest_headlines.heading: Understanding the Performance
digest_headlines.headline: Batch gain, overlap gain and disaggregation cost together decide each model's regime, and a per-layer model predicts throughput within 2.9% mean error.

digest_headlines.heading: System Implementation and Ablation
digest_headlines.headline: Ablations show fused MegaMoE cuts step latency 50% on Qwen3, two microbatches give the lowest latency, and disabling the coordinator costs 32% throughput.

digest_headlines.heading: Provisioning and Outlook
digest_headlines.headline: Speculative decoding contracts the optimal ratio, and SRAM expert accelerators would raise the modeled ceiling to 2.48× under speculation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior AFD studies are analytical or on older hardware, and this paper adds an end-to-end GB200 NVL72 audit.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: AFD ranges from parity to 1.17× over tuned wide EP, so the choice depends on provisioning rather than architecture.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists model specifications, complete standard-decode tables, residual errors, measurement rules, disaggregation comparison cells, and run presets.
